sources.title: Andrew Mathas, Hecke algebras and Schur algebras of the symmetric group, complete prepublication manuscript (author PDF of the 1998 notes; expanded published edition: Iwahori-Hecke Algebras and Schur Algebras of the Symmetric Group, AMS University Lecture Series 15, 1999); complete 79-page PDF.
sources.locator: Chapter 4 section 3 and Chapter 5 sections 2-4 of the complete 79-page manuscript, printed pp. 47-65: the Schur functor Proposition 4.19 and the reflection/conjugation dictionary (pp. 47-52); the Jantzen filtration setup and Lemmas 5.29-5.30 (pp. 54-58); Theorem 5.31 and Corollary 5.32 (q-Schaper, pp. 58-60); Lemma 5.34, Lemma 5.35, Theorem 5.36 and Corollary 5.37 with their proofs (pp. 60-63); the (4,3,2,1) 3-core example, Proposition 5.38 and the discussion before Theorem 5.40 (pp. 61-65).

contents.name: Chapter 4 section 3: the Schur idempotent, the corner eSe = H, and Proposition 4.19 (F(W^lambda) is the cell module, F(L^lambda) its head or zero)

Chapter 5 sections 1-2: the Jantzen filtration of the cell/Weyl modules, Lemma 5.29 (layer dimensions equal the Gram valuation) and Lemma 5.30 (semistandard weight dimensions detect virtual Weyl classes)
Theorem 5.31 (Jantzen sum formula for the q-Schur algebra) and Corollary 5.32 (q-Schaper) with the beta-sequence indexing of Lemma 5.26
Lemma 5.34: the e-core of a partition is well defined (the beta-number/abacus proof)
Lemma 5.35: if all composition factors of an S(d,n)-module lie in one block and [M] = sum a_lambda [W^lambda], then every W^lambda with a_lambda nonzero lies in that block

Theorem 5.36: Weyl modules W^lambda and W^mu lie in the same block if and only if lambda and mu have the same e-core, with the two-direction proof from the Jantzen sum formula and the linkage induction

Corollary 5.37 (Dipper-James, James-Mathas): the Hecke Specht modules S^lambda and S^mu lie in the same block if and only if their labels have the same e-core, proved with the decomposition End_H(M) = product End_{B_i}(M B_i)
Proposition 5.38 (James): for n = m + e with e-core gamma there are exactly e partitions in dominance order, with the adjacent bidiagonal decomposition pattern from the Jantzen computation
Printed p. 61 example: the 3-abacus of (4,3,2,1), its sequence of rim 3-hook removals and terminal 3-core (1)
The closing discussion before Theorem 5.40: classification of the irreducible Specht modules and general decomposition numbers remain open
contents.reason: The page deliberately states no open-problem remark of its own and no item consumes this boundary statement; the general decomposition-number boundary is already recorded on the published integral-Specht page and the batch-20 q-Schaper remark, so repeating it here would add a padding remark without a consumer.

contents.name: Theorems 5.39-5.40: the hook-valuation criterion for Weyl irreducibility and the e-restricted Specht irreducibility criterion under [n]!_{q-hat} nonzero
contents.reason: The irreducibility criteria are not part of the SYMR-8 declared inventory, no planned page consumes them, and stating them without the full lifting hypotheses of the source would overstate the page's scope, which stops at the e-core block classification and its weight-zero and weight-one consequences.

contents.name: Chapter 6 and the appendices of the 1999 AMS edition (canonical bases, adjustment matrices, modular branching)
contents.reason: These chapters are not part of the retrieved 1998 manuscript; the edition boundary is recorded, and canonical-basis, adjustment-matrix and branching material is owned by the planned KLR, Ariki and modular-branching pages of this same run, not by this pair.

sources.title: Stacey Law (lecturer), notes by Leonard Tomczak, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups, Cambridge Part III Michaelmas 2022 lecture notes; complete 76-page PDF.
sources.locator: Section 4.1 'James's Abacus', printed pp. 53-64: the beta-set definition with the shift X + l and the correspondence P(X) (Lemma 4.2); the e-abacus and Lemma 4.3; Lemmas 4.1 and 4.4 with Corollary 4.5 on row hook lengths; Corollary 4.6; Proposition 4.7 and Corollary 4.8 (hook removal as a bead slide); the definitions of e-core, e-quotient and weight with Lemma 4.9; Theorems 4.10-4.11; Proposition 4.12 and the worked e = 3 example; the quotient-tower material of section 4.2 onwards.

contents.name: Definition of a beta-set X, its l-shift X + l, the partition P(X), and Lemma 4.2 (the beta-sets for lambda are exactly X_lambda + l)
Definition of James's e-abacus and the bijection between beta-sets and bead configurations, with Lemma 4.3
Lemma 4.1 (row hook lengths from the first-column hook lengths), Lemma 4.4 and Corollary 4.5 (h is a row-i hook length exactly when h_i - h is a gap in X)
Proposition 4.7 (removing the hook H_{i,j} replaces X by (X minus {h_i}) union {h_i - h_{i,j}}) with its proof
Corollary 4.8 (a hook of length e exists exactly when a bead has an empty position below it on its runner; removing it slides the bead up one row)
Corollary 4.6 (a hook length divisible by e has an intermediate divisor hook of length e)
Definitions of an e-core partition, X^{(e)}_i, the e-quotient Q_e(lambda), the top-packed X^{(e)} and the e-core C_e(lambda), with the normalising condition e | |X|
Lemma 4.9 (shifting X by one permutes the runners cyclically and preserves the top-packed core) with the following remark on normalisation of the quotient
Theorem 4.10 (the e-core is the unique terminal partition of any e-hook removal sequence) with proof
Theorem 4.11 (bijection from the e-divisible hooks of lambda to the hooks of the e-quotient, |H| = e|f(H)| and Q_e(lambda minus H) = Q_e(lambda) minus f(H)) with proof
Proposition 4.12 (|lambda| = |C_e(lambda)| + e|Q_e(lambda)| and the hook-count identity) with proof

Worked example e = 3, lambda = (6,5,2,1^3): X_lambda = {11,9,5,3,2,1}, top-packed abacus, C_3(lambda) = (3,1), Q_3(lambda) = ((2,1),empty,(1)), four bead moves and two equivalent rim-hook removal orders
Section 4.2 onwards: quotient towers, Theorems 4.13/4.16, cores of the irreducible S_n-modules and the e-adic expansion
contents.reason: The quotient-tower recursion and core-of-irreducibles material is the combinatorial basis of the modular branching and residue-crystal pages of this run; this page's declared inventory stops at the e-core block classification with its weight-zero and weight-one consequences, so the tower is deferred to its consumer.

sources.title: William O'Donovan, A New Proof of Nakayama's Conjecture via Brauer Quotients of Young Modules, arXiv:1708.04365; complete 16-page preprint.
sources.locator: Section 1, pp. 1-6: the definitions of p-hook, p-core c_p(lambda) and p-weight, Theorem 1 and the surrounding discussion; the proof overview in section 5, pp. 13-14.

contents.name: Definition of p-hook, p-core c_p(lambda), p-weight, and the remark that the p-core is well defined by the abacus
Theorem 1: the blocks of the symmetric group are labelled by pairs (gamma,w) with gamma a p-core and n = |gamma| + pw, and S^lambda lies in (gamma,w) if and only if c_p(lambda) = gamma
Sections 2-5: the self-contained theory of Brauer quotients of Young modules, vertices, projective lifts and the inductive proof of Theorem 1
contents.reason: The Young-module/Brauer-quotient route needs the published vertices, Brauer-correspondence, Brauer-pair and projective-cover machinery of the representation-theory pages, and this page deliberately proves the classification by the q-Schur/Jantzen route; the source is registered as the independent treatment of the statement only.

sources.title: Sinead Lyle and Andrew Mathas, Blocks of affine and cyclotomic Hecke algebras, author-hosted complete preprint (published version in Math. Z.), PDF at the University of Sydney preprints page.
sources.locator: Section 2.1-2.3 of the complete 19-page preprint, pp. 4-7: the Ariki-Koike and cyclotomic Schur algebra setup, Lemmas 2.1-2.2 (Graham-Lehrer: composition factors of Specht and Weyl modules lie in one block) on pp. 4-5, Proposition 2.3 with its complete proof of the block correspondence between the Hecke and Schur algebras on pp. 4-5, Lemma 2.4 (linear independence of the Weyl classes) on p. 5, and Proposition 2.9 (blocks are the Jantzen equivalence classes) with proof on pp. 7-8.

contents.name: Lemma 2.4 (a virtual combination of Weyl classes vanishes if and only if every coefficient vanishes) with the K_0 framework of section 2.2

Proposition 2.3 with proof: S(lambda), S(mu) lie in the same block of the Hecke algebra if and only if the Weyl modules Delta(lambda), Delta(mu) lie in the same block of the Schur algebra, via the multiplicity comparison and the count of End_H(M)
Proposition 2.9 with proof: the Weyl modules lie in the same block exactly when they are Jantzen equivalent, using the Jantzen sum formula and the linear independence of the Weyl classes
Sections 2.4-4: cyclotomic Jantzen coefficients, the combinatorial classification for Ariki-Koike algebras, and the exceptional-parameter cases
contents.reason: The cyclotomic and affine refinement belongs to the planned cyclotomic-Hecke and KLR/Ariki pages of this run; this pair uses only the type-A block-correspondence propositions and does not state any cyclotomic classification.
